analysis.one_liner: Guarantees renewal of mining leases near the Boundary Waters and lets only Congress block mining there.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 216-204 on November 30, 2017, but the Senate never voted and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how federal mineral rights work in Minnesota's national forests. It would make it so only an Act of Congress—not the Interior Department—could withdraw minerals near the Boundary Waters from mining, bar the president from creating national monuments on those lands, and guarantee that certain mining leases are renewed for 20 years, then again in 10-year stretches. It names two specific hard-rock leases, the ones held by the Twin Metals copper-nickel project next to the Boundary Waters, and requires a pending environmental review of their renewal to be finished within 30 days.
analysis.who_benefits: The mining company holding the named leases, and copper-nickel mining interests generally: the bill locks in long-term, renewable federal mineral leases, makes it far harder for the government to ever withdraw the minerals from development, speeds the environmental review of lease renewal to 30 days, and lets the Interior Department grant surface-use permits to reach the deposits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The Twin Metals copper-nickel mining project

how_it_helps.text: Minerals in Minnesota's national forests could only be withdrawn from mining by an Act of Congress, taking that decision away from the Interior Department.

Two specific Superior National Forest hard-rock leases, MNES-01352 and MNES-01353, would be treated as indeterminate preference right leases, issued for 20 years and renewable in 10-year periods if the company complied with lease terms.
The Bureau of Land Management would have to complete the pending environmental assessment for renewing those two leases within 30 days of enactment.
The Interior Secretary could suspend lease operations when the mine could only run at a loss due to market conditions or strikes, protecting the lessee from losing the lease in a downturn.

analysis.who_pays: The public: national forest lands next to the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness—one of the country's most visited wilderness areas—would be locked toward sulfide-ore copper mining, a type of mining whose waste can permanently pollute water, and future administrations and presidents could no longer protect those minerals without a new law. The outdoor recreation economy built around clean water in northeastern Minnesota would bear the risk.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public lands near the Boundary Waters and its tourism economy

drawbacks.text: The bill ties the hands of future administrations: even if a president or Interior Secretary concluded that mining near the Boundary Waters posed unacceptable water risks, the minerals could only be protected by passing a law through Congress, which is far harder to do.

Requiring the environmental assessment of the two lease renewals to be completed within 30 days of enactment is an unusually short deadline for a federal review of mining next to a sensitive wilderness watershed.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill is that northeastern Minnesota's economy needs mining jobs, and the leases were issued before the withdrawal fight—supporters argued the government should honor its commitments rather than cancel them by executive action.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to one specific mining project and one industry, while the costs—long-term pollution risk to a world-class wilderness watershed and loss of the government's ability to protect it—are borne by the public indefinitely. The bill does exempt the Boundary Waters itself and keeps NEPA review in place, but it tilts every practical decision toward mining and makes protection nearly impossible to reinstate.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House on a near party-line vote, then sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee until the two-year Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 2, 2017 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee.
The committee ordered it reported by a vote of 17-13 and reported it on November 21, 2017.
The House passed the bill 216-204 on November 30, 2017, with 208 of 239 Republicans voting yes and only 8 of 194 Democrats voting yes.
The Senate received the bill on December 1, 2017 and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, existing protections for the Superior National Forest and the Boundary Waters watershed stayed in place and the government kept its authority to manage the minerals; the mining company had to pursue its leases through administrative decisions and the courts instead of getting a statutory guarantee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Boundary Waters and its clean-water economy

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split sharply by party: 208 of 239 Republicans voted yes while only 8 of 194 Democrats did, for a 216-204 margin; the bill's three cosponsors included one Democrat.

industries.industry: Copper-nickel (sulfide-ore) mining, specifically the Twin Metals project
industries.note: The bill names the two Superior National Forest leases held by Twin Metals—a subsidiary of Chilean mining company Antofagasta—and guarantees their long-term renewal, while making it nearly impossible for the government to withdraw the minerals from mining. Its gain comes from locking in access to public lands next to the Boundary Waters, where mining waste could contaminate the watershed that a recreation economy depends on.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and tourism in northeastern Minnesota (Boundary Waters outfitters and guides)
industries.note: The region's economy depends on clean water and an undisturbed wilderness that draws large numbers of visitors; the bill prioritizes mining rights next to that wilderness and shortens the environmental review, raising risk to the water the industry relies on.
